extracted.intended_audience: patent law scholars, IP practitioners, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for interpreting and drafting patent claims, including canonical sources (claims, specification, prosecution history), the role of dictionaries and skilled artisans, standards of review, and strategic drafting trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as best source for technical term
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best source for understanding a technical term is the specification from which it arose . . . .” (Multiform Desiccants, Inc. v. Medzam, Ltd., 133 F.3d 1473, 1478 (Fed. Cir. 1998)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the patent specification first when defining technical terms used in the claims; the specification provides authorial context and can be more reliable than general dictionaries for field-specific terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: “[T]he language of the claim frames and ultimately resolves all issues of claim interpretation.” (AbTox, Inc. v. Exitron Corp., 122 F.3d 1019, 1023 (Fed. Cir. 1997)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are the starting and controlling point for interpretation; other sources should be used to illuminate, not overwrite, claim text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim analysis as a legal question (appellate control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim analysis is to be treated as “purely legal” and “under the authority of the single appeals court” (517 U.S. 370, 391 (1996)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is principally a question of law for appellate resolution, though there is debate about the proper treatment of subsidiary factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review: de novo for documentary sources, clearly erroneous for factual predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument for de novo appellate review of documentary sources but a more deferential “clearly erroneous” standard for factual predicates (Anderson & Menell and related literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intrinsic documentary interpretation as reviewable de novo, while appellate courts should defer to trial-court factual findings (e.g., expert testimony about how a skilled artisan understands a term) absent clear error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to PTO as administrative alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should refer claim analysis questions to the PTO (John F. Duffy, On Improving the Legal Process of Claim Interpretation: Administrative Alternatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider administrative processes (PTO expertise and rulemaking) as mechanisms to improve predictability of dictionary selection and claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO may construe claims differently during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO has historically construed claims more broadly than courts do during infringement litigation; MPEP § 2111 and related commentary note this prosecutorial/litigation distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that claim meaning in prosecution may not match litigation constructions; drafters and litigators should account for differences in contexts and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction presumes textual imprecision
rubrics_metrics.description: “The process of claim construction itself presumes that the words of the claims are insufficiently precise to delineate those boundaries.” (Burk & Lemley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that claims may be indeterminate at their margins; construction is a method for resolving underdeterminacy rather than revealing a single pre-existing meaning in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting goal: as broad as the PTO will allow
rubrics_metrics.description: “The overall goal when drafting claims is to make them as broad as the Patent Office will allow.” (Merges & Duffy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim drafters should aim for maximal breadth subject to statutory and examination constraints, while balancing enforceability and validity risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth trade-off: broader claims increase invalidity risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad claim language increases the likelihood of the claim being invalidated, but patentees tend to favor broader language because courts have a bias against invalidating claims (Giles S. Rich; Roger Allan Ford; commentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing claim scope, weigh the commercial benefits of breadth against higher invalidity exposure; consider that litigation and institutional biases affect the practical desirability of broad claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation from viewpoint of skilled artisan
rubrics_metrics.description: “A patent presumes a readership skilled in the field of the invention.” (Ajinomoto Co. v. Archer-Daniels-Midland Co., 228 F.3d 1338, 1347 (Fed. Cir. 2000)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claim language as it would be understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing; technical dictionaries and expert evidence may inform that understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: No inquiry into subjective intent of applicant or PTO
rubrics_metrics.description: “No inquiry as to the subjective intent of the applicant or PTO is appropriate . . . .” (Markman v. Westview Instruments, Inc., 52 F.3d 967, 985 (Fed. Cir. 1995), aff’d 517 U.S. 370 (1996)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the parties’ or examiner’s subjective aims as the basis for claim meaning; focus on objective communicative content of the text and record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specification for linguistic context, not to rewrite claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have no objection to looking to the specification as part of the interpretative process. But our reason to look at the specification—for linguistic context—is very different from Judge Newman’s.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the specification to provide context and clarify meaning, but do not allow specification-based readings to impermissibly narrow or rewrite claim terms unless the patentee clearly disclaimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation vs construction is contested
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scholars and courts distinguish between 'interpretation' (linguistic meaning) and 'construction' (application to facts); others argue the distinction is artificial and that interpretation is ultimately an act of application (Merges & Duffy; Burk & Lemley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which framework you adopt: whether you treat textual meaning and application as distinct steps or as a unified interpretive act affects what sources and methods you prioritize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court role limited to interpretation, not rewriting for policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts interpret, rather than author, legal texts and should not 'rewrite' claims for fairness or policy reasons (United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers’ Coop.; Autogiro Co. of Am. v. United States; Salvano v. Merrill Lynch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist policy-driven reconstruction of claim language; when policy suggests changing scope, the proper remedy is legislation or administrative action, not judicial redefinition of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim meaning often dispositive of dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: “[T]o decide what the claims [legally] mean is nearly always to decide the case.” (Wang Labs., Inc. v. Am. Online, Inc., 197 F.3d 1377, 1381 (Fed. Cir. 1999)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that claim construction is frequently the determinative issue in infringement/invalidity disputes; invest appropriate effort in rigorous construction analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal lens: assess meaning as of filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim’s meaning is assessed as of the filing date (Playtex Prods., Inc. v. Procter & Gamble Co.; related authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing terms, use the knowledge and usage prevailing at the time of filing, not later developments in the art or language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence debate (dictionaries, experts, usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phillips en banc and associated commentary posed whether the public notice function of patent claims is better served by referencing primarily to technical and general purpose dictionaries and similar sources or by looking primarily to the patentee’s use of the term in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Phillips framework (intrinsic evidence primary) but acknowledge ongoing debate; use extrinsic sources (dictionaries, expert surveys, usage data) cautiously to confirm, not supplant, intrinsic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee intent useful narrowly; prefer reader-perspective analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: “Patentee intent at a lower level of generality is useful, because the understanding of the reader will depend on what the patentee intends to communicate through the language...we analyze the linguistic meaning from the perspective of the reader rather than the author.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor an objective reader-centered inquiry into what the patentee’s language would communicate to one skilled in the art; if invoking patentee intent, limit it to the intent as manifested by the written record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider purpose/functional context but weight linguistic clues
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority in Phillips gave great weight to linguistic considerations and less weight to the purpose of the invention, while dissenters emphasized purposive interpretation (discussion of baffle example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance purposive (what the invention was meant to accomplish) and linguistic/contextual clues; be explicit about how much weight you assign to each in a given construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of deliberate ambiguity by drafters
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators express concern that patent drafters can deliberately introduce ambiguity so later interpretation provides broader coverage (Retractable Techs.; Bessen & Meurer; Burk & Lemley; Osenga).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ambiguous language plausibly reflects strategic vagueness, scrutinize prosecution history and specification for disambiguating statements and consider the public-notice implications of accepting strategic ambiguity.
